cards.q: What are the four security control categories?
cards.a: Technical, Managerial, Operational, and Physical. Technical = implemented using systems; Managerial = administrative policies and procedures; Operational = implemented by people; Physical = limits physical access.

cards.q: Is a firewall a technical or managerial control?
cards.a: Technical. Technical controls are implemented using systems - operating system controls, firewalls, and anti-virus.

cards.q: Is a security policy a technical or managerial control?
cards.a: Managerial (administrative). Managerial controls are tied to security design and implementation - security policies and standard operating procedures.

cards.q: Are security guards and awareness programs operational or technical controls?
cards.a: Operational. Operational controls are implemented by people instead of systems - e.g., security guards and awareness programs.

cards.q: Name the six security control types.
cards.a: Preventive, Deterrent, Detective, Corrective, Compensating, and Directive. Examples: firewall (preventive), warning sign (deterrent), system logs (detective), backup recovery (corrective), block instead of patch (compensating), file storage policy (directive).

cards.q: Does a deterrent control directly prevent access?
cards.a: No. A deterrent discourages an intrusion attempt and makes an attacker think twice, but doesn't directly prevent access. Examples: application splash screens, threat of demotion, front reception desk, posted warning signs.

cards.q: Does a detective control always prevent access?
cards.a: No. A detective control identifies and logs an intrusion attempt but may not prevent access. Examples: collecting and reviewing system logs, reviewing login reports, patrolling the property, motion detectors.

cards.q: Restoring from backup after ransomware is what control type?
cards.a: Corrective. Corrective controls are applied after an event is detected to reverse its impact and continue operating with minimal downtime. Other examples: policies for reporting issues, contacting law enforcement, a fire extinguisher.

cards.q: A firewall rule that blocks a vulnerable app because it can't be patched yet is what control type?
cards.a: Compensating. A compensating control uses other means when existing controls aren't sufficient, and may be temporary. Other examples: separation of duties, simultaneous guard duties, a generator after a power outage.

cards.q: Is a directive control considered strong or weak?
cards.a: Relatively weak. A directive control directs a subject toward security compliance ('do this, please') - e.g., store sensitive files in a protected folder, compliance policies, user training, an 'Authorized Personnel Only' sign.

cards.q: A generator used after a power outage is what control type?
cards.a: Compensating, in the physical category. It controls the problem using other means when the primary control (utility power) isn't available.

cards.q: A door lock is what control type?
cards.a: Preventive, in the physical category. Preventive controls block access to a resource - 'you shall not pass.' Other preventive examples: firewall rules, guard shack ID checks.

cards.q: What does CIA stand for in the CIA Triad?
cards.a: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability - the fundamentals of security. It's sometimes referenced as the AIC Triad.

cards.q: Which part of the CIA triad does encryption primarily support?
cards.a: Confidentiality. Encryption encodes messages so only certain people can read them, preventing unauthorized information disclosure.

cards.q: Which part of the CIA triad does hashing primarily support?
cards.a: Integrity. Hashing maps data of any length to a fixed-length value; if the data changes, the hash changes, so modification is detected.

cards.q: Which part of the CIA triad does redundancy and fault tolerance support?
cards.a: Availability. Redundancy builds services that will always be available, and fault tolerance keeps a system running even when a failure occurs.

cards.q: What does integrity mean?
cards.a: Messages can't be modified without detection - data is stored and transferred as intended. Supported by hashing, digital signatures, certificates, and non-repudiation.

cards.q: Name three ways to provide confidentiality.
cards.a: Encryption (only certain people can read it), access controls (selectively restrict access to a resource), and two-factor authentication (additional confirmation before information is disclosed).

cards.q: Name four ways to provide integrity.
cards.a: Hashing, digital signatures (mathematically verify integrity), certificates (combined with a signature to verify an individual), and non-repudiation (proof of integrity, asserted to be genuine).

cards.q: Does patching support availability?
cards.a: Yes. Patching supports availability by improving stability and closing security holes. Redundancy and fault tolerance also support availability.

cards.q: What is non-repudiation?
cards.a: You can't deny what you've said - there's no taking it back. Like signing a contract: your signature proves you really did sign it. In cryptography it provides proof of integrity and proof of origin.

cards.q: Does a hash by itself associate data with an individual?
cards.a: No. A hash (message digest / fingerprint) only tells you if the data has changed. It doesn't associate the data with a person - that requires a digital signature.

cards.q: What three things does proof of origin (a digital signature) provide?
cards.a: Integrity (the message wasn't changed), authentication (proves the source), and non-repudiation (the signature isn't fake).

cards.q: Which key is used to create a digital signature?
cards.a: The sender's private key. Nobody else has that key, so nobody else can create that signature.

cards.q: Which key is used to verify a digital signature?
cards.a: The sender's public key. Any change to the message will invalidate the signature.

cards.q: Does a message need to be encrypted to be digitally signed?
cards.a: No. A signed message doesn't need to be encrypted - signing provides integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation, not confidentiality.

cards.q: What does the sender actually encrypt to create a digital signature?
cards.a: A hash of the plaintext. Alice hashes the message, encrypts that hash with her private key to make the digital signature, and sends it along with the plaintext.

cards.q: How does the recipient verify a digital signature?
cards.a: Bob decrypts the signature with Alice's public key to get the original hash, hashes the plaintext himself, and compares the two. If they match, the message is intact and came from Alice.

cards.q: What are the parts of the AAA framework (plus the step before it)?
cards.a: Identification (who you claim to be), Authentication (prove it), Authorization (what access you get), and Accounting (track resources used).

cards.q: Is a username identification or authentication?
cards.a: Identification - this is who you claim to be. It's usually your username. Proving it is the authentication step.

cards.q: Is a password identification or authentication?
cards.a: Authentication - proving you are who you say you are, using a password and other authentication factors.

cards.q: What does authorization determine?
cards.a: What access you have, based on your identification and authentication. Authorization models (roles, organizations, attributes) make this manageable.

cards.q: What does accounting track?
cards.a: Resources used - login time, data sent and received, and logout time.

cards.q: How do you authenticate a device that can't type a password?
cards.a: Put a digitally signed certificate on the device. The organization's CA signs it, and the CA's signature validates it - useful for VPN access and management software.

cards.q: Why use an authorization model instead of mapping users directly to resources?
cards.a: Mapping each user directly to resources doesn't scale and makes it hard to understand why access exists. A model (roles, organizations, attributes) adds abstraction, reduces complexity, and supports any number of users or resources.

cards.q: What is a gap analysis?
cards.a: A comparison of where you are with where you want to be - the 'gap' between the two. It evaluates people, processes, and systems against a baseline.

cards.q: Is a gap analysis usually quick?
cards.a: No. It can take weeks or months - an extensive study with numerous participants, data gathering, and technical research.

cards.q: Name two formal frameworks you might use as a gap analysis baseline.
cards.a: NIST SP 800-171 Rev 2 (protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in nonfederal systems) and ISO/IEC 27001 (information security management systems).

cards.q: What does ISO/IEC 27001 cover?
cards.a: Information security management systems. It's one of the formal standards an organization can use as the end goal for a gap analysis.

cards.q: What is the final output of a gap analysis?
cards.a: A gap analysis report - a formal description of the current state and recommendations for meeting the baseline. The path usually includes time, money, and lots of change control.

cards.q: What is the core idea of zero trust?
cards.a: Nothing is inherently trusted - everything must be verified. Zero trust is holistic: every device, process, and person, using MFA, encryption, permissions, additional firewalls, monitoring, and analytics.

cards.q: What are the two planes of operation in zero trust?
cards.a: The data plane (processes frames, packets, and network data) and the control plane (manages the data plane with policies and rules). This applies to physical, virtual, and cloud components.

cards.q: Which plane processes frames, packets, forwarding, and NAT?
cards.a: The data plane - processing, forwarding, trunking, encrypting, and NAT.

cards.q: Which plane manages routing tables, session tables, and policies?
cards.a: The control plane. It manages the data plane, defines policies and rules, and determines how packets are forwarded using routing, session, and NAT tables.

cards.q: What is the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)?
cards.a: The gatekeeper. It allows, monitors, and terminates connections between subjects (users, apps, non-human entities) and resources, and can be multiple components working together.

cards.q: Is the Policy Enforcement Point in the data plane or the control plane?
cards.a: The data plane. In the zero trust diagram, the subject's untrusted traffic passes through the PEP to the trusted enterprise resource, while the PDP sits in the control plane.

cards.q: What two components make up the Policy Decision Point (PDP)?
cards.a: The Policy Engine and the Policy Administrator. Together they form the Policy Decision Point - the process for making an authentication decision.

cards.q: Which PDP component evaluates access decisions and grants, denies, or revokes?
cards.a: The Policy Engine. It evaluates each access decision based on policy and other information sources, and grants, denies, or revokes.

cards.q: Which PDP component communicates with the PEP and generates access tokens?
cards.a: The Policy Administrator. It communicates with the PEP, generates access tokens or credentials, and tells the PEP to allow or disallow access.

cards.q: What is adaptive identity?
cards.a: Considering the source and the requested resources, using risk indicators like relationship to the organization, physical location, type of connection, and IP address. It can make authentication stronger if needed.

cards.q: What is threat scope reduction?
cards.a: Decreasing the number of possible entry points. It works alongside policy-driven access control, which combines adaptive identity with a predefined set of rules.

cards.q: What do bollards do?
cards.a: They prevent vehicle access while allowing people through, channeling people through a specific access point. They also identify safety concerns and can be used to an extreme (concrete barriers, moats).

cards.q: What is an access control vestibule?
cards.a: A set of doors where one door's state controls the others - e.g., opening one locks the others, or one can't be unlocked while another is open. It manages control through an area, one at a time or in controlled groups.

cards.q: What is two-person integrity/control?
cards.a: No single person has access to a physical asset. It minimizes exposure to an attack.

cards.q: Name four types of sensors used for physical security.
cards.a: Infrared (detects infrared radiation, common in motion detectors), pressure (change in force), microwave (movement across large areas), and ultrasonic (reflected sound waves).

cards.q: Which sensor detects movement across large areas?
cards.a: Microwave. Infrared is common in motion detectors, pressure detects force on floors and windows, and ultrasonic detects motion and collisions with sound waves.

cards.q: Which sensor detects a change in force on floors or windows?
cards.a: Pressure - used for floor and window sensors.

cards.q: What does CCTV stand for?
cards.a: Closed Circuit Television. It can replace physical guards; features like motion recognition and object detection (license plates, faces) are important, and cameras are networked and recorded over time.

cards.q: Does more lighting improve security?
cards.a: Yes. Attackers avoid the light, and non-IR cameras see better. Design matters: light levels, angles for facial recognition, and avoiding shadows and glare.

cards.q: What is a honeypot?
cards.a: A fake system that attracts attackers and traps them for observation. The 'attacker' is probably a machine. Most honeypot options are open source, and it's a constant battle to discern the real from the fake.

cards.q: What is a honeynet?
cards.a: A larger deception network with one or more honeypots - servers, workstations, routers, switches, firewalls. It provides more than one source of information.

cards.q: What is a honeyfile?
cards.a: A fake file with bait information (e.g., passwords.txt) placed on file shares. An alert is sent if it's accessed - a virtual bear trap.

cards.q: What is a honeytoken?
cards.a: Traceable fake data added to the honeynet so if it's stolen, you know where it came from. Examples: API credentials, fake email addresses, database records, browser cookies, web page pixels.

cards.q: Do honeytoken API credentials provide real access?
cards.a: No. They don't actually provide access - notifications are sent when they're used.

cards.q: Who gives final approval for a change in a formal process?
cards.a: The change control board. The typical process: request forms, purpose, scope, schedule, affected systems, risk analysis, CCB approval, then end-user acceptance after the change.

cards.q: Does the owner of a change usually perform the change?
cards.a: No. The owner (e.g., Shipping and Receiving for label printers) manages the process and receives updates; someone else, like IT, usually performs the change.

cards.q: What is a stakeholder in change management?
cards.a: Anyone impacted by the change who will want input. It may not be obvious - a shipping label software upgrade can affect shipping, accounting, delivery timeframes, and revenue recognition.

cards.q: What is an impact analysis?
cards.a: Determining a risk value (high, medium, low). Risks include the fix not working, breaking something else, OS failures, or data corruption - and also the risk of NOT making the change.

cards.q: Where should a change be tested before production?
cards.a: In a sandbox testing environment - no connection to the real world or production. Try the upgrade or patch there and confirm the backout plan, though a sandbox can't consider every possibility.

cards.q: What is a backout plan?
cards.a: A way to revert your changes and move everything back to the original. Some changes are difficult to revert, so always have good backups.

cards.q: What is a maintenance window?
cards.a: When the change happens. Workday changes affect production, so overnights are often better; the time of year matters too - retail networks are frozen during the holidays.

cards.q: Is a standard operating procedure a static document?
cards.a: No. It's a living document - the change process must be well documented (e.g., on the intranet) and updated as the process changes.

cards.q: Change management focuses on 'what'. What does the technical team focus on?
cards.a: 'How' to change it. Change management decides 'what' needs to change; the technical team executes the plan. There's no such thing as a simple upgrade.

cards.q: With an allow list, what can run?
cards.a: Only approved applications - nothing runs unless it's on the list. Very restrictive.

cards.q: With a deny list, what can run?
cards.a: Everything except items on the 'bad list.' Anti-virus and anti-malware work this way.

cards.q: Does a change approval give permission to make any change?
cards.a: No. The approval is very specific to the defined scope. If the scope needs to expand during the window, the change management process determines the next steps.

cards.q: What is a dependency?
cards.a: To complete A, you must complete B - a service needs another service, or an app needs a specific library version. Dependencies can span systems: upgrade the firewall code first, then the management software.

cards.q: Why use version control?
cards.a: To track changes to files or configuration over time and easily revert to a previous setting - router configs, Windows patches, registry entries. Some systems need extra software for this.

cards.q: What is a legacy application?
cards.a: An older application often no longer supported by the developer - you become the support team. Document it, create specific procedures for its quirks, and become the expert.

cards.q: What does PKI stand for?
cards.a: Public Key Infrastructure - the policies, procedures, hardware, software, and people to create, distribute, manage, store, and revoke digital certificates. It binds public keys to people or devices through a certificate authority.

cards.q: How many keys does symmetric encryption use?
cards.a: One single, shared key - a secret key algorithm. Encrypt and decrypt with the same key; if it gets out, you'll need another key.

cards.q: Is symmetric encryption faster or slower than asymmetric?
cards.a: Faster - less overhead than asymmetric encryption. It's often combined with asymmetric encryption.

cards.q: Does symmetric encryption scale well?
cards.a: No. The shared key can be challenging to distribute to everyone who needs it.

cards.q: Which key decrypts data encrypted with someone's public key?
cards.a: Only the matching private key. Example: Bob encrypts with Alice's public key, and Alice decrypts with her private key.

cards.q: Can you derive the private key from the public key?
cards.a: No. The key pair is generated together using randomization, large prime numbers, and lots of math, but the private key can't be derived from the public key.

cards.q: What is key escrow?
cards.a: A third party holds your decryption keys - possibly within your own organization. It can be legitimate (business or government access) but requires trust and carefully controlled conditions like court orders.

cards.q: What is another name for asymmetric encryption?
cards.a: Public key cryptography - two or more mathematically related keys: a private key you keep private and a public key anyone can see.

cards.q: Name two full-disk encryption tools.
cards.a: BitLocker (Windows) and FileVault (macOS). Full-disk and partition/volume encryption protect data at rest on SSDs, hard drives, USB drives, and more.

cards.q: What is EFS?
cards.a: Encrypting File System - Windows file-level encryption. Third-party utilities can also encrypt individual files.

cards.q: What is transparent database encryption?
cards.a: Encrypting all database information with a symmetric key.

cards.q: What is record-level database encryption?
cards.a: Encrypting individual columns, using separate symmetric keys for each column.

cards.q: Which VPN type is typically used for site-to-site?
cards.a: IPsec. Site-to-site VPNs encrypt all data between locations, regardless of the application.

cards.q: Which VPN type is typically used for client-based remote access?
cards.a: SSL/TLS. A client-based VPN encrypts all data from the device, regardless of the application.

cards.q: In cryptography, what is usually the only secret - the algorithm or the key?
cards.a: The key. The algorithm is usually a known entity; the key determines the output (encrypted data, hash, signature), so keep it private.

cards.q: Are asymmetric keys usually larger or smaller than symmetric keys?
cards.a: Larger. Symmetric keys of 128 bits or more are common; asymmetric keys of 3,072 bits or larger are common. Larger keys resist brute force.

cards.q: What is key stretching?
cards.a: Making a weak key stronger by processing it repeatedly - hash the password, hash the hash, and continue. Brute force would require reversing each hash, so attackers spend much more time.

cards.q: What is out-of-band key exchange?
cards.a: Sharing the key outside the network - telephone, courier, or in person. Don't send the symmetric key over the 'net.

cards.q: What is in-band key exchange?
cards.a: Sharing the key over the network, protected with additional encryption - commonly using asymmetric encryption to deliver a symmetric key.

cards.q: What is a session key?
cards.a: A random symmetric key the client encrypts with the server's public key. The server decrypts it and both use it to encrypt the session's data.

cards.q: What is an ephemeral key?
cards.a: A session key that is changed often. Session keys also need to be unpredictable.

cards.q: How can two parties create the same symmetric key without sending it?
cards.a: Each combines their own private key with the other's public key. Bob uses his private key + Alice's public key, Alice uses hers + Bob's public key, and both get the same symmetric key.

cards.q: What does TPM stand for?
cards.a: Trusted Platform Module - a specification for cryptographic functions built into a device, with a crypto processor, random number generator, and key generators.

cards.q: Is a TPM on the device or a separate appliance?
cards.a: On the device. It has persistent memory with unique keys burned in during manufacturing, and it's password protected with no dictionary attacks.

cards.q: What does a TPM commonly store securely?
cards.a: BitLocker keys, storage keys, and hardware configuration information, in its versatile memory.

cards.q: What does HSM stand for?
cards.a: Hardware Security Module - high-end cryptographic hardware as a plug-in card or separate device, used in large environments.

cards.q: TPM or HSM: which is used in large environments to store thousands of keys?
cards.a: HSM. HSMs serve clusters with redundant power, securely store thousands of keys, provide key backup, and include cryptographic accelerators.

cards.q: What is a cryptographic accelerator in an HSM?
cards.a: Hardware that offloads cryptographic CPU overhead from other devices.

cards.q: What does a key management system do?
cards.a: Manages all keys from one centralized console, separate from the data. It creates keys for services (SSL/TLS, SSH), associates keys with users, rotates them on intervals, and logs key use.

cards.q: What is a secure enclave?
cards.a: A protected area for secrets, often a hardware processor isolated from the main processor. It has its own boot ROM, monitors the boot process, a true RNG, real-time memory encryption, root keys, and hardware AES.

cards.q: What is obfuscation?
cards.a: Making something unclear and much harder to understand - but not impossible if you know how to read it. Examples: storing payment info without the card number, steganography.

cards.q: What is steganography?
cards.a: Greek for 'concealed writing' - hiding a message in plain sight (security through obscurity). It can be network-based (TCP packets), in images, audio, video, or invisible watermarks.

cards.q: What is the covertext?
cards.a: The container document or file that holds the hidden steganographic message.

cards.q: What is tokenization?
cards.a: Replacing sensitive data with a non-sensitive placeholder (e.g., an SSN replaced with a different number). Common in credit card processing - a captured token can't be reused later.

cards.q: Is tokenization a form of encryption or hashing?
cards.a: No. The original data and the token aren't mathematically related, so there's no encryption overhead.

cards.q: What is data masking?
cards.a: Hiding some of the original data to protect PII. It may only hide it from view (the data is intact in storage), controlled by permissions. Techniques: substituting, shuffling, encrypting, masking out.

cards.q: Are printer yellow dots an example of steganography?
cards.a: Yes - invisible watermarks are a common steganography technique.

cards.q: Is hashing one-way or two-way?
cards.a: One-way - it's impossible to recover the original message from the digest. That's why hashes are used to store passwords.

cards.q: Is a hash a fixed or variable length?
cards.a: Fixed length. Hash functions take input of any size and create a fixed-size message digest or checksum.

cards.q: What is a hash collision?
cards.a: Two different inputs producing the same hash. The hash should be unique, so collisions are a weakness.

cards.q: Which hash algorithm has a known collision problem?
cards.a: MD5 - collisions were found in 1996. Don't use MD5 for anything important.

cards.q: What is a salt?
cards.a: Random data added to a password when hashing. Every user gets their own salt, commonly stored with the password, so the same password creates a different hash.

cards.q: Do rainbow tables work against salted hashes?
cards.a: No. The extra random salt value means precomputed rainbow tables won't match.

cards.q: Does salting completely stop brute force?
cards.a: No. It slows down the brute force process but doesn't completely stop reverse engineering.

cards.q: Should you store passwords as plaintext or as a salted hash?
cards.a: A salted hash. Compare hashes during authentication - nobody ever knows your actual password.

cards.q: What is a blockchain?
cards.a: A distributed ledger that keeps track of transactions. Everyone on the network maintains the ledger, recording and replicating it to anyone and everyone.

cards.q: What links each block to the previous one?
cards.a: A hash calculated from the previous blocks of transaction data, added to the new block of verified transactions.

cards.q: What happens if a block is altered?
cards.a: Its hash and all following hashes are recalculated. The altered chain no longer matches the chains stored by the rest of the network, so it's rejected.

cards.q: Name some practical uses for blockchain.
cards.a: Payment processing, digital identification, supply chain monitoring, and digital voting.

cards.q: What is the standard format for digital certificates?
cards.a: X.509. Certificate details include serial number, version, signature algorithm, issuer, name of the cert holder, public key, and extensions.

cards.q: What does a digital certificate bind together?
cards.a: A public key with a digital signature and other details about the key holder. The signature adds trust - via Certificate Authorities in PKI, or other users in a Web of Trust.

cards.q: What does CA stand for?
cards.a: Certificate Authority - a trusted third party that digitally signs certificates. You trust the CA, therefore you trust the website. Third-party CAs are built into browsers.

cards.q: What is a CSR?
cards.a: A Certificate Signing Request. You create a key pair, then send the public key and identifying information to the CA to be signed.

cards.q: When creating a CSR, which key do you send to the CA?
cards.a: The public key. The private key stays with the applicant. The CA validates the request (e.g., confirms DNS emails and website ownership), signs the cert, and returns it.

cards.q: What is a root of trust?
cards.a: An inherently trusted component that other trust is built on - hardware, software, firmware, or a component such as an HSM, secure enclave, or Certificate Authority.

cards.q: What is a wildcard certificate?
cards.a: A certificate that applies to all server names in a domain, e.g., *.professormesser.com.

cards.q: What X.509 extension lets one certificate support many domain names?
cards.a: Subject Alternative Name (SAN). It lists additional identification information so one certificate can support many different domains.

cards.q: What does CRL stand for?
cards.a: Certificate Revocation List - maintained by the CA and can be a large file. After Heartbleed (2014), every affected certificate was replaced and the old ones moved to the CRL.

cards.q: What does OCSP stand for?
cards.a: Online Certificate Status Protocol. The browser checks revocation by sending a message to an OCSP responder, usually via HTTP.

cards.q: Is OCSP more or less efficient than downloading a CRL?
cards.a: More efficient than downloading a CRL. But not all browsers support it, and some support it but don't bother checking.

cards.q: What is OCSP stapling?
cards.a: The certificate holder verifies its own status: CA-signed status info is stored on the holder's server and 'stapled' into the SSL/TLS handshake, so the CA doesn't have to answer every client.

cards.q: Do self-signed / internal CA certificates need a public CA?
cards.a: No. Build your own CA, issue certificates signed by it, and install the CA certificate/trusted chain on all devices - they'll trust it exactly like a purchased certificate.

cards.q: Which threat actor has the highest sophistication and massive resources?
cards.a: Nation state. An external entity with constant attacks and massive resources, motivated by data exfiltration, philosophy, revenge, disruption, or war - targeting military, utilities, and financial control.

cards.q: What does APT stand for?
cards.a: Advanced Persistent Threat - commonly a nation state with constant attacks and massive resources.

cards.q: What was Stuxnet?
cards.a: A worm the United States and Israel used to destroy about 1,000 nuclear centrifuges - an example of nation-state sophistication.

cards.q: Which threat actor runs pre-made scripts without understanding them?
cards.a: Unskilled attacker. Anyone can do this - usually external, not sophisticated, with limited or no formal funding, motivated by disruption, data exfiltration, or sometimes philosophy. Looks for low-hanging fruit.

cards.q: Which threat actor is a hacker with a purpose (philosophical/political)?
cards.a: Hacktivist. Motivated by philosophy, revenge, or disruption; often external; can be remarkably sophisticated (DoS, website defacing, private document release); funding may be limited.

cards.q: Is an insider threat internal or external?
cards.a: Internal. Insiders are motivated by revenge or financial gain, have extensive resources (the organization's own), medium sophistication, and institutional knowledge - they know what to hit.

cards.q: What is the main motivation of organized crime?
cards.a: Money. Organized crime is very sophisticated ('the best hacking money can buy'), has lots of capital, and divides roles: one hacks, one manages exploits, one sells data, one handles customer support.

cards.q: What is shadow IT?
cards.a: Going rogue - working around the internal IT organization and building your own infrastructure, often in the cloud. Limited resources (company budget) and medium sophistication, may lack IT training.

cards.q: Is shadow IT internal or external?
cards.a: Internal. Shadow IT is part of the organization, unencumbered by IT roadblocks.

cards.q: Name three threat actor attributes.
cards.a: Internal/external (inside the house or trying to get in), resources/funding (none to extensive), and level of sophistication/capability (runs scripts vs. writes their own malware).

cards.q: Is organized crime usually internal or external?
cards.a: Almost always external. They're professional criminals motivated by money.

cards.q: What is a threat vector?
cards.a: The method an attacker uses to gain access to or infect a target - also called an attack vector. Security pros spend their careers protecting existing vectors and finding new ones.

cards.q: Why can SVG images be a threat?
cards.a: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphic) images are described in XML, so they can carry HTML injection or JavaScript attack code. Browsers must provide input validation to avoid running it.

cards.q: What is vishing?
cards.a: Phishing over the phone (voice). Other voice call vectors include spam over IP, war dialing, and call tampering.

cards.q: Why are USB devices a threat vector?
cards.a: They get around the firewall: malicious software on flash drives can infect air-gapped networks, USB devices can act as keyboards ('hacker on a chip'), and terabytes of data can walk out the door with zero bandwidth used.

cards.q: Is agentless software client-based?
cards.a: No. Agentless means no installed executable - the client runs a new instance each time, so compromised software on the server affects all users. Client-based software has its own vulnerabilities and needs constant updates.

cards.q: Why are unsupported systems a risk?
cards.a: They aren't patched - there may not even be an option. Eventually even the manufacturer won't help with outdated OSes, and a single system could be an entry point. Keep inventory current.

cards.q: Why do open service ports matter?
cards.a: Most services connect over a TCP or UDP port, and every open port is an opportunity for an attacker (app vulnerability or misconfiguration). More services expand the attack surface.

cards.q: What supply chain vector was used in the 2013 Target breach?
cards.a: Gaining access to the network using a vendor. Supply chain vectors also include managed service providers (one location into many customers) and counterfeit equipment with backdoors.

cards.q: What is phishing?
cards.a: Social engineering with a touch of spoofing, often delivered by email or text. Check the URL - usually something isn't quite right with spelling, fonts, or graphics.

cards.q: What is smishing?
cards.a: SMS (text message) phishing. Spoofing is a problem here too; it forwards links or asks for personal information.

cards.q: What is typosquatting?
cards.a: A type of URL hijacking using a misspelled domain, like professormessor.com instead of professormesser.com.

cards.q: What is pretexting?
cards.a: Lying to get information - the attacker is a character in a situation they create, e.g., 'Hi, we're calling from Visa regarding an automated payment...'

cards.q: What is business email compromise?
cards.a: Taking advantage of trust in email sources with spoofed addresses (professor@professormessor.com) for financial fraud - e.g., sending updated bank info to modify wire transfers, or links and malware attachments.

cards.q: What is impersonation?
cards.a: Attackers pretend to be someone they aren't - using reconnaissance details ('I'm with your help desk'), posing as someone higher in rank, throwing technical jargon around, or acting like a buddy.

cards.q: What is eliciting information?
cards.a: Extracting information from a victim without them realizing it - 'hacking the human.' Often seen with vishing, using well-documented psychological techniques instead of just asking for the password.

cards.q: Name four types of identity fraud.
cards.a: Credit card fraud, bank fraud, loan fraud (your info used for a loan or lease), and government benefits fraud (attacker obtains benefits on your behalf).

cards.q: What's the best protection against impersonation?
cards.a: Never volunteer information, don't disclose personal details, and always verify before revealing info - call back or verify through third parties. Verification should be encouraged.

cards.q: What is a watering hole attack?
cards.a: Infecting a third-party site the target group commonly uses (e.g., an industry site or local coffee shop), then infecting all visitors to reach the specific victims.

cards.q: When would an attacker use a watering hole attack?
cards.a: When the target is really secure - users don't respond to phishing or open attachments. The attacker has 'the mountain come to you,' which requires research.

cards.q: What's the defense against watering hole attacks?
cards.a: Defense in depth - firewalls and IPS to stop traffic, plus anti-virus/anti-malware signature updates. In the 2017 Polish Financial Supervision Authority attack, generic AV signatures caught the code.

cards.q: What is an influence campaign?
cards.a: Disseminating factually incorrect information to sway public opinion on political and social issues. Enabled through social media: create fake users and content, post, amplify, real users share, and mass media picks it up.

cards.q: What is brand impersonation?
cards.a: Pretending to be a well-known brand (Coca-Cola, McDonald's, Apple). Attackers create tens of thousands of sites with pop-ups ('You won!'); malware infection is almost guaranteed.

cards.q: Who commonly runs disinformation campaigns?
cards.a: Nation-state actors - to divide, distract, and persuade. Advertising is also an option to buy a voice for an opinion.

cards.q: What is memory injection?
cards.a: Adding code into the memory of an existing process to hide malware inside it and get access to that process's data, rights, and permissions.

cards.q: What is DLL injection?
cards.a: Attackers inject a path to a malicious DLL into a target process, so the DLL loads and runs as part of that process. One of the most popular memory injection methods - relatively easy to implement.

cards.q: What does DLL stand for?
cards.a: Dynamic-Link Library - a Windows library containing code and data that many applications can use.

cards.q: Can memory injection lead to privilege escalation?
cards.a: Yes. The injected code gets the same rights and permissions as the process, which can be used to perform a privilege escalation.

cards.q: What is a buffer overflow?
cards.a: Overwriting a buffer of memory so it spills into other memory areas - e.g., overflowing variable A changes the value of variable B.

cards.q: What should developers do to prevent buffer overflows?
cards.a: Perform bounds checking. Attackers spend a lot of time looking for openings.

cards.q: Is a buffer overflow a simple exploit?
cards.a: No. It takes time to avoid crashing things and to make the overflow do what the attacker wants.

cards.q: What makes a buffer overflow really useful to an attacker?
cards.a: Being repeatable - a repeatable buffer overflow means the system can be compromised.

cards.q: What is a race condition?
cards.a: A programming problem where things happen at the same time without planning, causing bad results - e.g., two users transferring money at once and the balances ending up wrong.

cards.q: What does TOCTOU stand for?
cards.a: Time-of-check to time-of-use.

cards.q: What is a TOCTOU attack?
cards.a: Something changes between when the system checks a value and when it uses the result of that check.

cards.q: Name a real-world race condition example.
cards.a: The Mars rover Spirit (2004) got stuck in a reboot loop from a file system problem, and at Pwn2Own 2023 a TOCTOU attack on a Tesla Model 3's infotainment via Bluetooth gained root.

cards.q: What should you always have before installing an update?
cards.a: A known-good backup. Also install updates only from trusted sources - not every update is equally secure.

cards.q: Should you install an update from a random pop-up?
cards.a: No. A random pop-up may not be legitimate - visit the developer's site directly. Many OSes only allow signed apps, so don't disable your security controls.

cards.q: What was the SolarWinds Orion attack?
cards.a: A supply chain attack reported in December 2020: attackers got into SolarWinds' development system and added malicious code to Orion updates, gaining access to hundreds of government agencies and companies.

cards.q: Why is the operating system a big target?
cards.a: Everyone has one, and it's remarkably complex - millions of lines of code mean more opportunities for security issues. The vulnerabilities are already there; we just haven't found them yet.

cards.q: When is Microsoft's Patch Tuesday?
cards.a: The 2nd Tuesday of each month. For example, May 9, 2023 had nearly 50 security patches, including 12 remote code execution vulnerabilities.

cards.q: Should patches be tested before deployment?
cards.a: Yes - a patch might break something else. Updates may also require a reboot (save your data), and you should have a fallback plan (a backup).

cards.q: What does SQLi stand for?
cards.a: SQL injection. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the most common relational database management system language.

cards.q: What is SQL injection?
cards.a: Putting your own SQL requests into an existing application - often from a web browser form or field. The application shouldn't allow this.

cards.q: What does adding ' OR '1'='1 to a query do?
cards.a: It's injected SQL that changes the query - it could let an attacker view all database information. SQLi can also delete data, add users, or cause a denial of service.

cards.q: What is the root cause of code injection?
cards.a: Bad programming - the application doesn't properly handle input and output.

cards.q: Name four data types that can be injected.
cards.a: HTML, SQL, XML, and LDAP - there are many different injectable data types.

cards.q: What does XSS stand for?
cards.a: Cross-site scripting (not CSS, which is Cascading Style Sheets). It was originally called 'cross-site' because information from one site could be shared with another.

cards.q: What language does XSS commonly use?
cards.a: JavaScript.

cards.q: XSS takes advantage of whose trust?
cards.a: The trust a user has for a site. It's one of the most common web app vulnerabilities.

cards.q: What is a reflected (non-persistent) XSS attack?
cards.a: The site allows scripts in user input (often a search box). The attacker emails a link with a script; it runs in the victim's browser as if from the server and sends credentials, session IDs, or cookies to the attacker.

cards.q: What is a stored (persistent) XSS attack?
cards.a: The attacker posts a malicious payload (e.g., on a social network). It's persistent - everyone who views the page gets it, so it can spread quickly.

cards.q: What's the developer's main defense against XSS?
cards.a: Validate input - don't allow users to add their own scripts to an input field. Users should also avoid untrusted links and keep browsers updated.

cards.q: What is firmware?
cards.a: The software inside the hardware - the operating system of the device. Only the vendor can fix it, if they know about the problem and care to fix it (e.g., Trane thermostat fixes took up to two years).

cards.q: What is the difference between EOL and EOSL?
cards.a: EOL (end of life): the manufacturer stops selling but may still support it. EOSL (end of service life): support is no longer available - no ongoing security patches, though premium support may exist.

cards.q: How do you protect legacy platforms that can't be updated?
cards.a: Add security protections like additional firewall rules and IPS signatures for older OSes. The risk of running end-of-life software needs to be compared to the return.

cards.q: What is VM escape?
cards.a: Breaking out of a virtual machine to interact with the host operating system or hardware. Example: Pwn2Own 2017 chained an Edge bug, a Windows 10 kernel bug, and a VMware hardware simulation bug.

cards.q: Why is VM escape so serious?
cards.a: Once you escape, you can control the host and the other guest VMs - full control of the virtual world.

cards.q: What is a resource reuse vulnerability?
cards.a: The hypervisor reuses resources (RAM, storage, CPU) between VMs, so data can inadvertently be shared between them. Updated memory management and security patches mitigate the risk.

cards.q: What manages the relationship between physical and virtual resources?
cards.a: The hypervisor - it allocates available RAM, storage, and CPU among the VMs.

cards.q: What is directory traversal?
cards.a: An attack where faulty configurations put data at risk. Other cloud service attacks include DoS, authentication bypass, and remote code execution.

cards.q: What is an out-of-bounds write?
cards.a: Writing to unauthorized memory areas, which can cause data corruption, crashing, or code execution.

cards.q: What CVSS score is considered high or critical?
cards.a: 7.0 and above. Per the notes, 63% of code in production had unpatched high or critical vulnerabilities.

cards.q: Name two widely exploited web application vulnerabilities mentioned in the notes.
cards.a: Log4j and Spring Cloud Function - web application attacks that are easy to exploit with extensive rewards.

cards.q: Why is the supply chain a risk?
cards.a: It has many moving parts (raw materials, suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, customers). Attackers can infect any step without suspicion because people trust their suppliers, and one exploit can infect the entire chain.

cards.q: How should you reduce hardware supplier risk?
cards.a: Use a small supplier base for tighter control, enforce strict policies and procedures, and make security part of the overall design. There's a limit to trust.

cards.q: Is open source software immune to supply chain attacks?
cards.a: No - the source code itself can be compromised.

cards.q: What should you verify when installing software?
cards.a: The digital signature during initial installation. Also consider how secure updates and patches are, since some are automatic.

cards.q: What happened with counterfeit Cisco equipment (2022)?
cards.a: In July 2022, DHS arrested a reseller CEO who sold over $1 billion of fake Cisco products made in China through 30+ companies since 2013 - until they started breaking and catching fire.

cards.q: What caused the 2017 Verizon data exposure?
cards.a: A third party left an Amazon S3 data repository open, exposing 14 million records. Open permissions are increasingly common with cloud storage.

cards.q: Should users log in directly as root?
cards.a: No. Disable direct login to the root account and use su or sudo. Accounts with root or administrator access should be protected, and there shouldn't be many of them.

cards.q: Is Telnet secure?
cards.a: No - Telnet sends all traffic in the clear. Use SSH. You can verify with a packet capture.

cards.q: Is FTP encrypted?
cards.a: No. FTP, Telnet, SMTP, and IMAP send traffic in the clear - use encrypted versions like SFTP, SSH, and IMAPS.

cards.q: What did the Mirai botnet exploit?
cards.a: Default configurations on IoT devices (60+ defaults) - cameras, routers, doorbells, garage door openers. Mirai was released as open-source software.

cards.q: What is it called to gain full OS access on Android?
cards.a: Rooting. It installs custom firmware that replaces the OS, giving uncontrolled access that circumvents security features.

cards.q: What is it called to gain full OS access on iOS?
cards.a: Jailbreaking. Like rooting, it circumvents security and makes the MDM relatively useless.

cards.q: What is sideloading?
cards.a: Installing apps manually without using an app store. Malicious apps are a big concern - one Trojan horse can create a data breach.

cards.q: What happens to MDM control when a device is jailbroken?
cards.a: The MDM becomes relatively useless because jailbreaking circumvents its security features.

cards.q: What is a zero-day attack?
cards.a: An attack on a vulnerability the vendor doesn't know about - there's no patch or mitigation. It's a race between exploiting the vulnerability and creating a patch.

cards.q: What does CVE stand for?
cards.a: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (cve.mitre.org).

cards.q: Why are zero-days hard to defend against?
cards.a: It's difficult to defend against the unknown - attackers keep newly found holes to themselves for personal gain, and the vendor has no fix.

cards.q: What does ransomware do?
cards.a: Encrypts your data files (pictures, documents, music, movies) and demands payment through an untraceable system for the decryption key - an unfortunate use of public-key cryptography.

cards.q: Does ransomware usually leave the OS working?
cards.a: Yes. The OS remains available - 'they want you running, but not working.'

cards.q: What is the best protection against ransomware?
cards.a: Always have a backup - an offline backup, ideally. Also keep the OS, applications, and anti-virus/anti-malware signatures up to date.

cards.q: What is a drive-by download?
cards.a: Malware installed just by visiting a web page. Your computer must run a program to get malware - email links, pop-ups, drive-by downloads, or worms.

cards.q: Does a virus need user action to spread?
cards.a: Yes - it needs you to execute a program. It then reproduces through file systems or the network. Some viruses are invisible, some are annoying; keep anti-virus signatures updated.

cards.q: Does a worm need user action to spread?
cards.a: No. A worm self-replicates and self-propagates using the network as its transmission medium, so it can take over many systems very quickly.

cards.q: Name four virus types.
cards.a: Program viruses (part of an application), boot sector viruses, script viruses (OS and browser-based), and macro viruses (common in Microsoft Office).

cards.q: Where are macro viruses common?
cards.a: Microsoft Office documents.

cards.q: What is a fileless virus?
cards.a: A stealth attack that operates in memory and is never installed as a file, avoiding anti-virus detection. Typical flow: user clicks a link, a vulnerability launches PowerShell, scripts run in memory, and an auto-start is added to the Registry.

cards.q: What can mitigate worm infestations at the network level?
cards.a: Firewalls and IDS/IPS - but they don't help much once the worm gets inside.

cards.q: What is spyware?
cards.a: Malware that spies on you for advertising, identity theft, or affiliate fraud. It tricks you into installing it (peer to peer, fake security software), monitors browsing, and can include keyloggers.

cards.q: What is bloatware?
cards.a: Apps preinstalled by the manufacturer that you didn't expect or need. They use storage space, may slow the system, and could open it to exploits.

cards.q: What's the first option for removing bloatware?
cards.a: The built-in uninstaller. Some apps have their own uninstaller; third-party uninstallers and cleaners are probably not the first option - always have a backup.

cards.q: What is a keylogger?
cards.a: Malware that saves all your input (website URLs, passwords, emails) and sends it to the attackers. Other data logging includes clipboard, screen, instant messaging, and search queries.

cards.q: Does encryption protect against a keylogger?
cards.a: No. A keylogger circumvents encryption because your keystrokes are captured in the clear.

cards.q: What is a logic bomb?
cards.a: Malicious code that waits for a predefined event, often left by someone with a grudge. A time bomb triggers on a time or date; a logic bomb on a user event. Difficult to identify and to recover from.

cards.q: Are logic bombs easy to find with signatures?
cards.a: No - each is unique, so there are no predefined signatures. Real examples: South Korea (2013) wiped storage and boot records; Ukraine's power substation (2016) logic bomb disabled circuits.

cards.q: What is a rootkit?
cards.a: Malware (originally a Unix technique) that modifies core system files as part of the kernel, making it invisible to the OS (e.g., not in Task Manager) and to traditional anti-virus.

cards.q: What helps protect against rootkits at boot?
cards.a: Secure boot with UEFI (security in the BIOS). Also look for the unusual with anti-malware scans and use a remover specific to the rootkit.

cards.q: How can you help prevent logic bombs?
cards.a: Formal change control processes, electronic monitoring that alerts on changes (host-based intrusion detection, Tripwire), and constant auditing, since an admin can circumvent existing systems.

cards.q: If someone has physical access to a server, how much control do they have?
cards.a: Full control - an OS can't stop an in-person attack. Door locks keep out the honest people; there's always a way in.

cards.q: What is RFID cloning?
cards.a: Copying an RFID access badge or key fob - duplicators cost under $50 on Amazon and copying takes seconds.

cards.q: What's the defense against RFID cloning?
cards.a: MFA - use another authentication factor along with the card.

cards.q: Name three environmental attack targets.
cards.a: Power (monitoring), HVAC and humidity controls (large data centers must be cooled), and fire suppression.

cards.q: What is a DoS attack?
cards.a: Forcing a service to fail by overloading it or exploiting a design failure or vulnerability. It can be for competitive advantage or as a smokescreen for another exploit - or as simple as turning off the power.

cards.q: What is the difference between DoS and DDoS?
cards.a: DDoS (distributed) launches an army of computers - usually a botnet - to use all the bandwidth or resources. The Zeus botnet infected over 3.6 million PCs.

cards.q: What is DDoS amplification?
cards.a: Turning a small attack into a big one by reflecting it off Internet services with little authentication, like NTP, DNS, and ICMP.

cards.q: Why is DDoS called an asymmetric threat?
cards.a: It's an asymmetric threat - the attacker may have fewer resources than the victim.

cards.q: Give an example of an unintentional DoS.
cards.a: A layer 2 loop without STP, downloading multi-gigabyte files over a slow DSL line, or a water line break.

cards.q: Name three ways to perform DNS poisoning.
cards.a: Modify the DNS server (crafty hacking), modify the client's hosts file, or send a fake response to a valid DNS request (an on-path attack with real-time redirection).

cards.q: Does the hosts file take precedence over DNS?
cards.a: Yes - the host file takes precedence over DNS queries, so modifying it redirects the client.

cards.q: What is domain hijacking?
cards.a: Getting access to the domain registration to control where traffic flows - no need to touch the servers. In 2016, attackers changed 36 Brazilian bank domains and 'became the bank' for 6 hours.

cards.q: What is URL hijacking?
cards.a: Making money from people's typing mistakes: selling the misspelled domain to the owner, redirecting to a competitor, phishing sites, or drive-by downloads.

cards.q: Is professormesser.org vs .com an example of typosquatting?
cards.a: Yes - typosquatting with a different top-level domain. Other types: outright misspelling, a typing error, or a different phrase.

cards.q: What is a wireless deauthentication attack?
cards.a: A significant wireless DoS that disconnects users using unprotected 802.11 management frames - the original standards sent them in the clear with no authentication or validation.

cards.q: Which IEEE standard protects wireless management frames?
cards.a: 802.11w (July 2014). It encrypts important management frames like disassociate, deauthenticate, and channel switch announcements. It's required for 802.11ac compliance.

cards.q: Does 802.11w encrypt beacon frames?
cards.a: No. Beacons, probes, authentication, and association frames aren't encrypted.

cards.q: What is RF jamming?
cards.a: A DoS that transmits interfering signals to decrease the signal-to-noise ratio, so the receiver can't hear the good signal. Types include constant random bits, legitimate frames, random timing, and reactive jamming.

cards.q: Is a microwave oven disrupting Wi-Fi 'jamming'?
cards.a: No - that's interference. Jamming is intentional: someone wants your network to not work.

cards.q: What is 'fox hunting'?
cards.a: Tracking down a jamming source with the right equipment - a directional antenna and attenuator. Jammers need to be close to be effective.

cards.q: What was an on-path attack formerly called?
cards.a: Man-in-the-middle. The attacker redirects your traffic, then passes it on to the destination - you never know it was redirected.

cards.q: What is ARP poisoning?
cards.a: An on-path attack on the local IP subnet - ARP has no security, so fake ARP replies redirect traffic through the attacker.

cards.q: What is an on-path browser attack?
cards.a: Malware/Trojan on the victim's own computer does the proxy work (formerly man-in-the-browser). It's easy to proxy encrypted traffic, everything looks normal, and it waits for you to log in to your bank.

cards.q: Is a replay attack an on-path attack?
cards.a: No - the actual replay doesn't require the original workstation. The attacker first gets raw network data (network tap, ARP poisoning, malware) and replays it to appear as someone else.

cards.q: What is pass the hash?
cards.a: The attacker captures a username and password hash during authentication and sends their own authentication request using the captured credentials.

cards.q: What is session hijacking (sidejacking)?
cards.a: Sidejacking: the victim authenticates, the server provides a session ID, and the attacker intercepts it and uses it to access the server as the victim. Session IDs are often stored in cookies.

cards.q: What's the best defense against session hijacking?
cards.a: Encrypt end-to-end (HTTPS) - they can't capture your session ID if they can't see it. At least encrypt end-to-somewhere (e.g., a personal VPN) to avoid capture on local wireless.

cards.q: Are browser cookies executable?
cards.a: No. Cookies store info for tracking, personalization, and session management - not generally a security risk unless someone gets access to them, though they can be a privacy risk.

cards.q: What vulnerability did WannaCry exploit?
cards.a: Windows SMBv1 - the executable exploited it for arbitrary code execution.

cards.q: What attack hit British Airways' checkout pages?
cards.a: Cross-site scripting - 22 lines of malicious JavaScript on checkout pages stole information from 380,000 victims.

cards.q: What attack breached the Estonian Central Health Database?
cards.a: SQL injection - it breached healthcare information for an entire country.

cards.q: What is privilege escalation?
cards.a: Gaining higher-level access to a system by exploiting a bug or design flaw - commonly the highest-level access. These are high-priority patches. Example: CVE-2023-29336 (Win32k) gave SYSTEM privileges.

cards.q: What is horizontal privilege escalation?
cards.a: User A can access User B's resources (same level, different user).

cards.q: What does DEP stand for and do?
cards.a: Data Execution Prevention - only data in executable areas can run. It's a privilege escalation mitigation, along with patching quickly and updated anti-malware.

cards.q: What does ASLR stand for and do?
cards.a: Address Space Layout Randomization - it prevents a buffer overrun at a known memory address.

cards.q: What does CSRF/XSRF stand for?
cards.a: Cross-site request forgery - also called a one-click attack or session riding, and pronounced 'sea surf.'

cards.q: CSRF takes advantage of whose trust?
cards.a: The trust a web application has for the user's browser. Requests (like posting a status or transferring funds) are made without the user's consent or knowledge.

cards.q: How do you prevent CSRF?
cards.a: Add anti-forgery techniques to the application - usually a cryptographic token to prevent a forgery.

cards.q: What is directory traversal?
cards.a: Reading files from a web server outside the website's file directory (path traversal) - e.g., browsing the Windows folder. Caused by web server software or web application code vulnerabilities.

cards.q: What is a birthday attack?
cards.a: Finding a hash collision by brute force - generating multiple versions of plaintext until the hashes match. Like 23 students having about a 50% chance of sharing a birthday.

cards.q: How do you protect against birthday attacks?
cards.a: Use a large hash output size.

cards.q: What is a downgrade attack?
cards.a: Forcing systems to use weaker encryption instead of perfectly good encryption.

cards.q: What was POODLE?
cards.a: A 2014 on-path downgrade attack (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) forcing clients to fall back to SSL 3.0. Because of POODLE, modern browsers won't fall back to SSL 3.0.

cards.q: What is SSL stripping?
cards.a: An on-path attacker rewrites URLs so the victim talks HTTP to the attacker while the attacker talks HTTPS to the server - capturing credentials like usernames and passwords.

cards.q: What is password spraying?
cards.a: Trying a few of the most common passwords against an account, then moving to the next account - no lockouts, no alarms, no alerts.

cards.q: What is a brute force attack?
cards.a: Trying every possible password combination until the hash is matched. A strong hashing algorithm slows things down.

cards.q: Online vs offline brute force: which is slowed by account lockouts?
cards.a: Online: keep trying the login - very slow and most accounts lock out. Offline: obtain the list of users and hashes, then calculate and compare hashes - needs large computing resources but no lockouts.

cards.q: Should passwords ever be stored in plaintext?
cards.a: No. Anyone with access to a plaintext password file has every credential. If your app stores plaintext passwords, get a better application.

cards.q: What does IOC stand for?
cards.a: Indicator of Compromise - an event that indicates an intrusion with high confidence ('he's calling from inside the house').

cards.q: What is impossible travel?
cards.a: Logins from places too far apart for the time between them - e.g., Omaha, then Melbourne three minutes later. It's easy to catch with log analysis and automation.

cards.q: Why would an attacker block security update sites?
cards.a: To stay as long as possible ('play keep-away'). Blocked content includes auto-update connections, links to security patches, third-party anti-malware sites, and removal tools.

cards.q: Why are missing logs suspicious?
cards.a: Logs are evidence, so attackers try to cover their tracks by removing them (authentication, file access, firewall, proxy, server logs). Logs should be secured and monitored.

cards.q: What is out-of-cycle logging?
cards.a: Log activity at an unexpected time - e.g., OS patching outside the normal patch day (the attacker keeping other attackers out) or unusual firewall log activity.

cards.q: Name some common IOCs.
cards.a: Unusual network activity, changes to file hash values, irregular international traffic, changes to DNS data, uncommon login patterns, and spikes of read requests to certain files.

cards.q: Is concurrent session usage from multiple locations an IOC?
cards.a: Yes. Multiple interactive logins from multiple locations by one user is suspicious - though it can be hard to track with multiple devices and automated processes.

cards.q: Name three reasons to segment a network.
cards.a: Performance (high-bandwidth apps), security (users shouldn't talk directly to database servers), and compliance (mandated segmentation like PCI, which also makes change control easier).

cards.q: What does an ACL do?
cards.a: Allows or disallows traffic or access based on groupings like source IP, destination IP, port number, time of day, or application. ACLs also restrict access to network devices and list file permissions.

cards.q: Name four ways an application allow list can identify apps.
cards.a: Application hash (unique identifier), certificate (signed apps from certain publishers), path (only run apps in these folders), and network zone (apps can only run from this zone).

cards.q: Can you lock yourself out with an ACL?
cards.a: Yes - be careful when configuring ACLs on network devices.

cards.q: What is an out-of-band update?
cards.a: An emergency update outside the normal schedule for zero-day and important security discoveries. Normal patching includes monthly updates and third-party (app and driver) updates.

cards.q: What is least privilege?
cards.a: Setting rights and permissions to the bare minimum needed. All user accounts and applications should be limited, and users shouldn't run with admin privileges - it limits the scope of malicious behavior.

cards.q: What happens to a device that fails configuration enforcement / posture assessment?
cards.a: It's quarantined - often on a private VLAN with limited access - then rechecked after corrections. The posture check covers OS patch version, EDR version and status, firewall status, and certificate status.

cards.q: Should decommissioning be a formal policy?
cards.a: Yes. Don't throw data in the trash - someone will find it. It mostly applies to storage devices (hard drives, SSDs, USB drives), which can be recycled for another system or destroyed.

cards.q: In monitoring, what is the difference between sensors and collectors?
cards.a: Sensors gather data (IPS, firewall logs, authentication logs, web server, database, and email logs). Collectors aggregate it (proprietary consoles, SIEM, syslog), and many SIEMs have a correlation engine.

cards.q: What does EDR stand for?
cards.a: Endpoint Detection and Response - a lightweight endpoint agent that detects threats, investigates them (root cause analysis), and responds (isolate, quarantine, roll back) automatically via API.

cards.q: Does EDR rely only on signatures?
cards.a: No - it also uses behavioral analysis, machine learning, and process monitoring to scale to the growing number of threats.

cards.q: What does HIPS stand for?
cards.a: Host-based Intrusion Prevention System. It recognizes and blocks known attacks using signatures, heuristics, and behavior - e.g., buffer overflows, registry updates, writing files to the Windows folder. Often built into endpoint protection.

cards.q: What tool can verify open ports?
cards.a: Nmap or a similar port scanner. Close every port except required ones, control access with a firewall (ideally an NGFW), and keep monitoring.

cards.q: Why remove unnecessary software?
cards.a: All software has bugs, some are security vulnerabilities, and every app has a different patching process. Removing unused software reduces risk - an easy fix.

cards.q: What does a host-based firewall control?
cards.a: Incoming and outgoing application traffic on each endpoint, controlled by application process. It can identify and block unknown processes to stop malware, and is managed centrally.

cards.q: What does a cloud responsibility matrix show?
cards.a: Who is responsible for which security tasks - the cloud provider or the customer - across IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, etc. Most providers publish one so everyone knows up front; it varies by provider and contract.

cards.q: In IaaS, who manages the operating system?
cards.a: The customer. In IaaS the provider manages the physical hosts, network, and datacenter; the customer manages the OS, applications, network controls, and everything above.

cards.q: In SaaS, who manages the application?
cards.a: The provider. In SaaS the provider manages applications, network controls, OSes, and physical infrastructure; the customer still manages data, devices, and accounts.

cards.q: Is information and data always the customer's responsibility?
cards.a: Yes - in SaaS, PaaS, IaaS, and on-prem, information and data, devices, and accounts and identities are customer managed.

cards.q: What is a hybrid cloud?
cards.a: More than one public or private cloud. It adds complexity: network protection mismatches (authentication, firewall, server settings), different security monitoring, and data leakage across the public Internet.

cards.q: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
cards.a: Describing servers, network, and applications as code. You can version it like application code and build other instances the same way every time - a perfect version every time.

cards.q: What is serverless architecture?
cards.a: Function as a Service (FaaS): apps are split into autonomous functions running in stateless compute containers, possibly event-triggered and ephemeral. The OS is removed from the equation and managed by a third party.

cards.q: What is a monolithic application?
cards.a: One big application that does everything - UI, business logic, data input and output. It has a large codebase and change control challenges.

cards.q: What is the 'glue' between microservices?
cards.a: APIs (Application Programming Interfaces). Microservices are scalable (scale just what you need), resilient (outages are contained), and have containment built in for security and compliance.

cards.q: What is an air gap?
cards.a: Physical isolation - devices aren't connected (e.g., an air gap between Switch A and Switch B). They must be connected directly or through another switch/router to communicate.

cards.q: Can VLANs communicate with each other without a router?
cards.a: No. VLANs are separated logically instead of physically, and can't communicate without a Layer 3 device / router.

cards.q: What does SDN stand for?
cards.a: Software Defined Networking - splitting a network device's functions into separate logical units (data, control, management planes). It's perfectly built for the cloud.

cards.q: What are the three SDN planes?
cards.a: Infrastructure layer / data plane (forwarding, trunking, encrypting, NAT), control layer / control plane (routing, session, NAT tables, dynamic routing updates), and application layer / management plane (configure and manage).

cards.q: Which SDN plane handles SSH, browser, and API configuration?
cards.a: The management plane (application layer) - configuring and managing the device with SSH, a browser, or an API.

cards.q: Does each VM have its own operating system?
cards.a: Yes - each application instance gets its own guest OS on top of a hypervisor. That adds overhead and complexity, making virtualization relatively expensive.

cards.q: Do containers have their own OS kernel?
cards.a: No. A container holds the code and dependencies to run an app as an isolated sandboxed process, but uses the host kernel - lightweight, portable, with secure separation between apps.

cards.q: Centralized vs decentralized security management: which has a single point of failure?
cards.a: Centralized. It gives correlated alerts, consolidated log analysis, and comprehensive status and patching - but it's a single point of failure with potential performance issues.

cards.q: What does SCADA stand for?
cards.a: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition - large-scale, multi-site industrial control systems where a PC manages equipment for power generation, refining, manufacturing, and logistics.

cards.q: What does ICS stand for?
cards.a: Industrial Control Systems - SCADA is a large-scale, multi-site ICS.

cards.q: How should SCADA/ICS be protected?
cards.a: Extensive segmentation - no access from the outside. These distributed control systems provide real-time information and system control.

cards.q: What does RTOS stand for?
cards.a: Real-Time Operating System - a deterministic processing schedule with no time to wait for other processes. Used in industrial equipment, automobiles, and military environments, and extremely sensitive to security issues.

cards.q: What is an embedded system?
cards.a: Hardware and software designed for one specific function or as part of a larger system, optimized for size and/or cost - e.g., traffic light controllers, digital watches, medical imaging systems.

cards.q: What is a common IoT weakness?
cards.a: Weak defaults - IoT manufacturers are not security professionals. IoT includes sensors, smart devices, wearables, and facility automation.

cards.q: Is redundancy the same as high availability?
cards.a: No. Redundant equipment may need to be powered on manually; high availability is always on, always available - possibly many components working together (active/active). Higher availability almost always costs more.

cards.q: What does MTTR stand for?
cards.a: Mean Time to Repair - commonly used to reference resilience.

cards.q: What is resilience?
cards.a: Whether you can maintain availability and recover - and how quickly - when something happens. It depends on the root cause, replacement hardware, patch availability, and redundant systems.

cards.q: Is cybersecurity insurance risk transference?
cards.a: Yes - risk transference. It can cover attacks and downtime (popular with ransomware), recover internal losses, and limit the cost of legal proceedings from customers.

cards.q: What is elasticity?
cards.a: How quickly and easily capacity can increase or decrease (scalability) - possibly many times a day. Security monitoring needs to scale too.

cards.q: How do you protect a device you can't patch, like a time clock?
cards.a: Add security controls around it - e.g., a firewall for your time clock. Embedded systems like HVAC controls and time clocks often aren't designed for end-user updates.

cards.q: What provides short-term vs long-term backup power?
cards.a: A UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) for short-term and generators for long-term backup power. Primary power may come from one or more providers.

cards.q: Why use security zones instead of IP address ranges?
cards.a: Zone-based security is more flexible and secure than IP address ranges. Each network area joins a zone (trusted/untrusted, inside/Internet/screened) and policies become simple, like 'Untrusted to Screened.'

cards.q: What is the attack surface?
cards.a: All the ways into your 'house' - application code, open ports, the authentication process, and human error. Everything can be a vulnerability.

cards.q: Name three ways to minimize the attack surface.
cards.a: Audit the code, block ports on the firewall, and monitor network traffic in real time.

cards.q: Where do honeypots usually sit in a zone design?
cards.a: In the screened zone. In the notes diagram, a firewall sends anomalous traffic to the honeypots while normal traffic goes to servers.

cards.q: What is fail-open?
cards.a: When a system fails, data continues to flow.

cards.q: What is fail-closed?
cards.a: When a system fails, data does not flow.

cards.q: Is IPS typically active or passive?
cards.a: Active - connected inline so traffic passes through it and can be allowed or denied in real time.

cards.q: Is IDS typically active or passive?
cards.a: Passive - a copy of the traffic is sent to it through a tap or port monitor, so it can't block in real time.

cards.q: Can passive monitoring block traffic in real time?
cards.a: No - it only examines a copy of the network traffic.

cards.q: What's the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
cards.a: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) sends an alarm or alert; an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) stops the attack before it gets into the network. Both watch for exploits like buffer overflows and XSS.

cards.q: What is a jump server?
cards.a: A highly secured, hardened, and monitored device that provides access into a secure network zone. Admins SSH/tunnel/VPN to it, then jump from there - so compromising it is a significant breach.

cards.q: What is a forward proxy?
cards.a: An 'internal proxy' that protects and controls user access to the Internet. The user sends requests to the proxy, which makes them on the user's behalf.

cards.q: What is a reverse proxy?
cards.a: A proxy for inbound traffic from the Internet to your internal service, sitting in front of the web server.

cards.q: What is an open proxy?
cards.a: A third-party, uncontrolled proxy - a significant security concern, often used to circumvent existing security controls.

cards.q: Explicit vs transparent proxy?
cards.a: Explicit: applications need to know how to use (be configured for) the proxy. Transparent: invisible to the user. Proxies help with caching, access control, URL filtering, and content scanning.

cards.q: Is NAT a type of proxy?
cards.a: Yes - NAT is one of the simplest 'proxies,' a network-level proxy. Most proxies are application proxies that understand how the application works (HTTP, HTTPS, FTP).

cards.q: Active/active vs active/passive load balancing?
cards.a: Active/active: all servers share the load (with TCP/SSL offload, caching, QoS, content switching). Active/passive: some servers are on standby and take over if an active server fails.

cards.q: What is SSL offload on a load balancer?
cards.a: The load balancer handles encryption/decryption so the servers don't have to. Load balancing distributes load across servers, is invisible to users, and provides fault tolerance.

cards.q: What is 802.1X?
cards.a: Port-based Network Access Control (NAC) - you don't get network access until you authenticate. Used with an authentication database like RADIUS, LDAP, TACACS+, or Kerberos, on wired and wireless.

cards.q: What does EAP stand for?
cards.a: Extensible Authentication Protocol.

cards.q: Is EAP a protocol or a framework?
cards.a: An authentication framework with many RFC-based ways to authenticate; manufacturers can build their own EAP methods. EAP integrates with 802.1X.

cards.q: In 802.1X, what is the supplicant?
cards.a: The client requesting access.

cards.q: In 802.1X, what is the authenticator?
cards.a: The device that provides access, such as a switch or wireless access point.

cards.q: In 802.1X, what is the authentication server?
cards.a: The server that validates the client credentials (e.g., RADIUS).

cards.q: Traditional firewalls filter at which OSI layer?
cards.a: Layer 4 - filtering by port number. Most network firewalls are also layer 3 devices at the network edge with NAT, VPN, and dynamic routing authentication.

cards.q: NGFWs filter at which OSI layer?
cards.a: Layer 7 (the OSI application layer) - every packet's data is analyzed and categorized before a security decision is made.

cards.q: What does UTM stand for?
cards.a: Unified Threat Management - an all-in-one security appliance combining URL filter/content inspection, malware inspection, spam filter, router/switch, firewall, IDS/IPS, bandwidth shaper, and VPN endpoint.

cards.q: Name other names for an NGFW.
cards.a: Application layer gateway, stateful multilayer inspection, and deep packet inspection. NGFWs control traffic by application, apply app-specific IPS signatures, and filter URLs by category.

cards.q: What does a WAF protect?
cards.a: Web applications - a WAF applies rules to HTTP/HTTPS conversations and allows or denies based on expected input, blocking attacks like SQL injection.

cards.q: Which compliance standard focuses heavily on WAFs?
cards.a: PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) - WAFs are a major focus.

cards.q: What does a VPN concentrator do?
cards.a: Encrypts and decrypts VPN traffic. It's often integrated into a firewall and can be specialized hardware or software.

cards.q: Which port does an SSL/TLS VPN use?
cards.a: TCP 443 - so there are (almost) no firewall issues.

cards.q: Does an SSL/TLS VPN require digital certificates or shared passwords like IPsec?
cards.a: No. It authenticates users without requiring digital certificates or shared passwords like IPsec, and can run from a browser or a light VPN client.

cards.q: Is a site-to-site IPsec VPN usually on-demand or always-on?
cards.a: Always-on (or almost always). Firewalls often act as the VPN concentrators on each side. SSL/TLS VPNs, by contrast, are usually on-demand remote access.

cards.q: What does SD-WAN stand for?
cards.a: Software Defined Networking in a Wide Area Network - a WAN built for the cloud, letting cloud apps communicate directly to the cloud without hopping through a central data center.

cards.q: Does SD-WAN adequately address security?
